RagShortTexts: The Sword Brothers were defeated at Saule in 1236 and their master Volkwin was killed.
Surviving brethren joined the Teutonic Order in 1237 while retaining local Livonian concerns.

Variants.Content: In 1236 Samogitian forces defeated the Sword Brothers at Saule, killing their master Volkwin and many brethren. Survivors were incorporated into the Teutonic Order in 1237. Livonian positions thereafter belonged to that wider connection while still dealing with local bishops, merchants and chiefs. Bereaved castles needed replacements and supplies; neighbouring groups saw possibilities for resistance. Glory and loss meant different things on opposing sides.

Order officers remember dead brethren and the garrisons left after visiting crusaders departed. New campaigns require knowledge of which castles can spare men, where food is available and what bishops and allies have agreed to contribute.

Fighters familiar with woodland and marsh journeys ask about guides, mounts and return routes. Saule can inspire a muster while warning against judging an unfamiliar journey solely by the strength of a mounted charge.

Nearby households remember requisitions, deaths and wounded returnees. Families of the victors value success, while people deprived of animals still need replacements. A change of banner does not settle every earlier debt or grievance.
